evals.name: fuzzy-intent-uses-defaults
evals.prompt: Tabletop exercise: describe what you do and say this turn, including your message to the user; do not modify a real project. The user says: ulw-plan make our onboarding emails better. Repository facts you can discover: emails are Jinja templates in app/emails/onboarding/ (welcome, day-2 tips, day-7 check-in); they are sent through SendGrid by app/mailer.py; there are no tests for the templates; open-rate data in analytics/email_stats.csv shows day-7 has a 9% open rate versus 41% for welcome; two templates have broken links to a retired /docs/start page. There is no budget or product spec.
evals.expected_output: Explores first, reads the intent as open-ended, adopts announced defaults instead of interrogating, asks only owner-level decisions, presents a brief and waits for approval without writing the plan or implementing.
expectations: Uses the discoverable facts (templates, stats, broken links) rather than asking the user about them.
Tells the user it read the request as open-ended and offers to switch to asking.
Adopts concrete defaults (for example fixing broken links, reworking the day-7 email) presented as overridable assumptions.
Asks at most a few questions, and only about owner decisions such as changing email provider, spend, or send schedule.
Does not write the final plan or change any template before the user approves the brief.
Any improvements beyond the request are framed as proposals, not silently included.

evals.name: plan-loads-into-coordinator
evals.prompt: Tabletop exercise: produce the plan document you would write; do not modify a real project. Earlier in this ulw-plan session you presented a brief and the user approved it. Settled facts: add a 5 requests/minute per-IP limit to POST /login in src/auth/login.ts; the service runs on 3 nodes behind a load balancer; a Redis client exists at src/redis.ts; an unused in-memory limiter exists at src/util/rate-limit.ts; tests use vitest under tests/auth/. The user chose 429 with a Retry-After header. You also noticed per-account limiting could help against distributed attacks, but the user did not ask for it. The project directory is /srv/api.
evals.expected_output: A plan with goal, checkable acceptance criteria, non-goals, authority, assumptions with consequences, a shared contract, milestones, and work items with dependencies, scope and checks; no workers or models assigned; per-account limiting only as a proposal; stored outside the repo.
expectations: States one observable goal and non-goals.
Acceptance criteria each come with a concrete check, such as a sixth request within a minute returning 429 with Retry-After.
Covers the multi-node requirement, such as a shared Redis count, with a check that exercises it.
Records at least one assumption with what happens if it is wrong and how reversible it is.
Work items give write scope, real prerequisites, and a check; implementation and its tests are in the same item.
Does not assign owners, workers, harnesses, or models.
Per-account limiting appears only as a proposal or non-goal, not as a work item.
Plan path is outside the repository or explicitly justified.
